Steering hydrogen evolution in CO 2 electroreduction through tailoring
various co-catalysts
Xian-Zong Wang, Subiao Liu, Qingxia Liu, Jing-Li Luo
⁎
Department of Chemical and Materials Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta T6G 1H9, Canada
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Carbon dioxide reduction reaction
Hydrogen evolution reaction
Carbon support material
Ag nanowires
A B S T R A C T
Electrochemical CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) is a sustainable approach to producing carbon-neutral fuels
when combined with renewable energies. Besides the emphatic consideration of developing efficient catalysts, a
suitable conductive carbon agent served as co-catalyst with a low activity toward the competitive hydrogen
evolution reaction (HER), is also highly needed. However, there have been limited studies focused on the in-
vestigation of co-catalyst during CO 2 RR, especially on their HER behavior. We herein explored the HER of
various co-catalyst, i.e., acetylene black (AB), carbon black (CB) and graphite flake (GF) as well as carbon
nanotube (CNT), and their composites with sub-25 nm Ag nanowires (NWs) as catalysts. GF and CB exhibit a
higher activity toward CO 2 RR and HER, respectively. In contrast, CB/Ag NWs achieve the highest Faraday
efficiency and partial current density for CO 2 RR, whereas CNT/Ag NWs prefer HER. The differences in HER
suggest a critical influence of co-catalyst and this study points to a better guidance on the selection of co-catalyst
for CO 2 RR.
text.body:
1. Introduction
Converting CO 2 to useful chemicals is considered as a sustainable
pathway to mitigate the environmental issues caused by the increased
atmospheric CO 2 concentration [1,2]. Electrocatalytic CO 2 reduction
reaction (CO 2 RR) holds the potential to relieve the greenhouse gas ef-
fect, especially when combined with the utilization of renewable energy
sources, e.g., wind and solar energies [3,4]. Currently, substantial
materials such as nanostructured metals [5-7], metal oxides [8,9],
carbon-based materials [10,11] and molecular complexes [12,13] have
been experimentally and/or computationally explored for CO 2 RR. In
addition to a high-performance catalyst, a superior conductive agent or
co-catalyst is also of prime importance [12,14]. For example, Zhang
et.al compared the catalysis activity of cobalt phthalocyanine combined
with different carbon support, including CNT, CB and reduced graphene
oxide (rGO). Their results showed that CNT rather than CB or rGO
combined with cobalt phthalocyanine structures achieve higher effi-
ciency and selectivity in reducing CO 2 to CO [12]. Also, it is reported
that CF has improved the uniformity of Ag nanoparticles distribution as
well as higher activity and efficiency for CO 2 conversion to CO than
these with CB or graphene nanoplates [14]. Moreover, Jin et al. in-
vestigated the role of carbon support in high selectivity involving the
ultrasmall Au nanocatalysts on the nitride carbon for electrocatalytic
CO 2 reduction [15]. These researches confirm the critical influence of
carbon support materials on the selectivity of the aim products. It is
well-known that the simultaneous occurrence hydrogen evolution re-
action (HER) inevitably reduces the selectivity of the aimed products,
this means that a suitable co-catalyst possessing a low catalytic activity
toward HER is preferred for the purpose of improving the selectivity
and Faraday efficiency (FE) [12,16]. Therefore, it is imperative and
meaningful to screen the co-catalyst which in turn facilitates the CO 2 RR
when incorporated with the high-performance catalysts.
Nanostructured carbon materials, i.e., carbon black [7], reduced
graphene oxide [17], graphene nanosheet [18], carbon foam [14] and
carbon nanotube [12], have been selected as the representative co-
catalyst. Despite the fact that remarkable progress has been achieved
for CO 2 RR over various catalysts, limited studies have focused on the
co-catalyst [6,14], particularly on their HER behaviors. Lately, our
group prepared 5-fold twinned Ag nanowires (NWs) with diameters less
than 25 nm and achieved high catalytic activity and selectivity for
electrochemical CO 2 RR to CO-rich syngas [5]. The good performance of
the Ag NWs makes it a suitable catalyst as a case study to explore the
influence of co-catalyst on the HER behaviors.
This study investigated the activities of various carbon support
material, i.e., acetylene black (AB), carbon black (CB), graphite flake
(GF) and carbon nanotube (CNT), with and without loaded Ag NWs as
the catalysts, i.e., AB/Ag NWs, CB/Ag NWs, GF/Ag NWs and CNT/Ag
NWs, toward HER and CO 2 RR. Compared with the pure carbon agents,

2. Experimental
2.1. Specifications of carbon materials, chemicals and gases
The synthesis process of Ag NWs can be found in our previous work
[5]. All the chemicals, AB (Soltex, Inc.), CB (Cabot Corp. vxc72), GF
(Angstron Materials, Inc.), CNT (multi-walled, Sigma-Aldrich), Nafion
perfluorinated ion-exchange resin solution (Sigma-Aldrich), Nafion® N-
117 membrane (Alfa Aesar), Glassy carbon electrode (GCE, AIDA Sci-
ence Technology Company, China), CO 2 (99.999%, Praxair) are of
analytical grade and used without further purification.
2.2. Electrochemical measurements
10 mg of carbon material without/with 10 mg of Ag NWs was dis-
persed in 1 mL mixed solvent: isopropanol (700 μL), Nafion solution
(200 μL) and deionized water (100 μL). This mixed solvent was ultra-
sonicated for 3 h to form a homogeneous ink. Then, 25 μL ink was
loaded onto GCE (0.785 cm 2 ) and dried overnight in air at room tem-
perature before testing. Three electrodes system was applied with sa-
turated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, a platinum
gauze as the counter electrode and the GCE as the working electrode.
The electrolyte is 0.1 M KHCO 3 aqueous solution saturated with CO 2
(pH = 6.8) at room temperature. Prior to and throughout the tests, the
electrolyte was saturated by bubbling CO 2 at a flow rate of 20 mL/min.
The potentiostatic polarization measurements were conducted with a
Solartron 1255 frequency response analyzer. All potentials are reported
with respect to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The gas

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Pure carbon agents toward CO production
Fig. 1a, b and c present the static total current densities (j), partial
current densities of CO (j CO ), FEs of AB, CB and GF, and CNT. In the
potential window from -0.66 to -1.06 V, CB and GF have a higher j CO
than those of AB and CNT (Fig. 1b). GF possesses the highest FEs
(Fig. 1c) for CO production and the largest j CO of GF (Fig. 1b) among the
four co-catalysts. As the potential shifts to the negative values, CB and
CNT exhibit an increasing stage, followed by a decreasing stage. The
FEs of AB increase slowly and achieve a maximum FE of 21.1%. Con-
currently, at a fixed potential of -0.96 V, the j CO of GF and CB is over
2.8-fold higher than those of AB and CNT (Fig. 1d). GF has a 1.5-fold
and 2-fold higher FE than those of AB and CNT, respectively. The higher
j CO and FE of GF suggests its good catalytic activity toward CO 2 RR.
Fig. 1e shows the Tafel plots of the four carbon agents for elucidating
their intrinsic activities of CO 2 RR to CO. GF exhibits a smaller Tafel
slope (157 mV/dec), remarkably closer to the theoretical value
(~118 mV/dec) than those of CB, AB and CNT, indicating a higher
intrinsic activity of GF toward CO 2 RR [19,20]. Additionally, CB ex-
periences negligible degradation and GF exhibits a slight increase of j,
whereas AB and CNT show notable current increase, an indication of a
better stability of the CB and GF (Fig. 1f). Conclusively, GF, followed by
CB, possesses the highest j CO and FE among the four co-catalysts.
3.2. Pure carbon agents toward HER
Because HER and CO 2 RR are often interconnected, Fig. 2a and b
present the j H2 and the corresponding FEs, respectively. Apparently, CB
exhibits a remarkably higher j H2 and FEs than those of the other three
agents (Fig. 2a). The FEs of CB and GF show a decreasing trend upon
negatively shifting the potential (Fig. 2b). Specifically, the FEs of CB
decrease from 72.3% at -0.66 V to 36.6% at -1.16 V. In contrast, the
FEs of AB show two stages and reach a peak value of 45.0% at -0.96 V.
Concurrently, at a fixed potential of -1.06 V, the j H2 of CB (0.55 mA/
cm 2 ) is 1.6, 1.3, and 3-fold higher than those of AB, GF, and CNT, re-
spectively (Fig. 2c). Meanwhile, the FE of CB (43.6%) is 1.3 and 1.5-fold
higher than those of GF and CNT, respectively. By comparing the Tafel
plot of j H2 (Fig. 2d) and j CO (Fig. 1e), both AB and CNT have the
comparable values for H 2 and CO production, suggesting their poor
selectivity for H 2 or CO. However, the slopes of CB (514 mV/dec) and
GF (378 mV/dec) for H 2 production are 2.4 and 2.7-fold higher than
those of 190 and 157 mV/dec for CO production, respectively. The
lower Tafel slopes for CO production, rather than for H 2 , highlight the
good selectivity of CB and GF toward CO.
3.3. Carbon/Ag NWs composites toward CO production
To examine the influences of co-catalysts on the practical appli-
cation of CO 2 RR toward CO production, a case study was conducted
by coupling the sub-25 nm Ag NWs with the co-catalysts. Generally,

AB/Ag NWs and CB/Ag NWs have the higher js than those of GF/Ag
NWs and CNT/Ag NWs (Fig. 3a). As compared to the pure carbon at
-1.16 V (Fig. 1b), a remarkable increase of j CO is achieved (Fig. 3b).
Significant increases of js CO of the four carbon/Ag NWs composites
suggest the remarkable catalytic activity of Ag NWs. The net increase
in j CO of CB/Ag NWs (3.92 mA/cm 2 ) is 2.1-fold higher than that of
CNT/Ag NWs (1.93 mA/cm 2 ), suggesting the high activity of CB/Ag
NWs. The maximum FEs of CB/Ag NWs (99.2%, -0.96 V), followed
by that of AB/Ag NWs (90.5%, -0.96 V), are 17% and 24% higher
than those of GF/Ag NWs (82.3%, -0.86 V) and CNT/Ag NWs
(75.6%, -0.76 V), respectively (Fig. 3c). Ag NWs coupled with var-
ious carbon materials are electrochemically active to drive CO 2 RR to
CO with high catalytic activity and selectivity. This activity perfor-
mance was believed to originate from the ultrathin Ag NWs with a
diameter of less than 25 nm (diameter effect) together with the
energetically favorable (100) facet completely enclosed the Ag NWs
(facet effect) [5]. Moreover, when the potential is more negative than
-0.76 V, the FEs of CB/Ag NWs are over 85%, indicating that CB/Ag
NWs selectively promote the CO 2 RR rather than HER. In contrast, a
significant decrease of FEs was observed for CNT/Ag NWs, from
75.6% (-0.76 V) to 50.1% (-1.16 V). Specifically, at a fixed po-
tential of -1.06 V, the j CO of CB/Ag NWs (3.22 mA/cm 2 ) is 48% and
86% higher than 2.17 mA/cm 2 of GF/Ag NWs and 1.73 mA/cm 2 of
CNT/Ag NWs, respectively (Fig. 3d). Consistently, the FE of CB/Ag
NWs (89.4%) is 1.3 and 1.6-fold higher than those of GF/Ag NWs
(69.9%) and CNT/Ag NWs (57.1%), respectively. The Tafel plot
slopes of the composites (Fig. 3e) are considerably smaller than those
of pure carbons (Fig. 1e), especially for the CNT/Ag NWs and AB/Ag
NWs. The long-term test indicates the better stability of CB/Ag NWs
and GF/Ag NWs than those of AB/Ag NWs and CNT/Ag NWs (Fig. 3f).

3.4. Comparison of carbon/Ag NWs composites and pure carbon toward
HER
To gain a better insight into the coupling effect between the carbon
agents and catalyst, the j H2 values of pure carbon and their composites
with Ag NWs are compared at every specific potential (Fig. 4). In
comparison to the AB, the j H2 of AB/Ag NWs decreases from -1.16 to
-0.86 V, whereas it increases at -0.76 and -0.66 V (Fig. 4a), im-
plying that the Ag NWs inhibit the HER at more negative potentials
while enhancing the HER at more positive potentials. Significant in-
hibition effect is observed for CB/Ag NWs, their j H2 is lower than that of
CB throughout the entire potential range (Fig. 4b). However, the j H2 of
CNT/Ag NWs is significantly higher, from 5.5-fold at -1.16 V to 2.5-
fold at -0.66 V, than those of CNT (Fig. 4d), which highlights the
Fig. 4. A comparison of j H2 of (a) AB and AB/Ag NWs, (b) CB and CB/Ag NWs, (c) GF and GF/Ag NWs, and (d) CNT and AB/Ag NWs at various potentials. (e) Raman
spectra of AB, CB, GF, and CNT.

text.body:
considerable promotion effect of Ag NWs toward HER when combined
with CNT. Similarly, the j H2 values that are 1.5 and 2-fold higher are
observed for GF/Ag NWs at -1.06 and -1.16 V, respectively, in-
dicating that the GF/Ag NWs remarkably promote the HER when the
potential is more negative than -1.06 V (Fig. 4c). Consequently, CB/Ag
NWs achieve the highest FE for CO production, while CNT/Ag NWs
possess the largest j H2 . These changes of j H2 suggest that the coupling
effect between carbon agents and Ag NWs is potential and material
dependent. For comparing the difference between the various carbon
support materials, Raman spectroscopy were used to investigate the
local disorder and crystallinity of four carbon materials. Fig. 4e shows
the characteristic D and G bands at about 1340 and 1575 cm -1 , re-
spectively. The ration of D-and G-band intensity (I D /I G ) is sensitive to
structure defects is calculated accordingly. The D band arises from the
disordered sp 2 hybridized carbon, while G band is associated with the
CeC tangential stretching mode and indicates the presence of crystal-
line graphitic carbon [21]. From the Raman spectrum shown in Fig. 4e,
a larger value of I D /I G was observed for AB and CB than these for GF
and CNT, indicating that AB and CB have a higher disorder degree.
Considering the Ag NWs coupled with carbon materials are more active
toward CO 2 RR than HER, a higher defective carbon material is favor-
able for CO formation and thus lead to higher coverage of the coad-
sorbed CO. According to the literature [22], the presence of coadsorbed
CO would lead to two predominant effects on the HER activity of a
metal catalyst. Firstly, the coadsorbed CO will weaken the binding
strength between H and the catalyst surface, and thus change the ex-
posed surface's inherent HER activity (poison effect). Also, the coad-
sorbed CO will block active sites for HER since the formed CO partially
covers the catalyst surface, resulting in a decreased availability of the
catalyst surface for HER. Therefore, the intrinsic property of Ag (with
very weak hydrogen binding) [23] together with the poisoning effect of
CO contributes to the suppression of HER. Therefore, a large ratio of I D /
I G enhances CO formation and thus, inhibits the HER. It could be pro-
posed that a larger I D /I G is more favorable toward CO 2 RR.
4. Conclusions
This work studied the catalytic activities of AB, CB, GF, and CNT as
well as their composites with Ag NWs toward CO 2 RR and HER.
Although the four composites exhibit high catalytic activity toward
CO 2 RR, their activities toward HER vary with the co-catalysts. The
changes of j H2 suggest that the coupling effect between the co-catalysts
and Ag NWs varies with the agent being used. CB/Ag NWs remarkably
inhibit HER throughout the entire potential range. In contrast, the HER
of CNT/Ag NWs is significantly enhanced. Similarly, GF/Ag NWs pro-
mote the HER when potential is more negative than -1.06 V. AB/Ag
NWs inhibit the HER at more negative potentials while enhancing the
HER at more positive potentials. Therefore, CB/Ag NWs achieve the
highest j CO while CNT/Ag NWs possess the largest j H2 . CB is a suitable
co-catalyst for CO 2 RR when combined with Ag NWs. Analysis of the
Raman spectra of the four carbon materials implies that a larger I D /I G is
more favorable to the CO 2 RR and thus, leads to a suppression of HER.
The results of this study reveal the non-negligible influence of the co-
catalysts on CO 2 RR and offer a guidance for the selection of co-catalysts
for electrochemical CO 2 conversion.
